stories.teaser: A mother’s volunteer network now helps Israelis in trouble in 49 countries
stories.headline: Friends Rescuing Friends: a volunteer network founded by a bereaved mother now helps Israelis in emergencies in 49 countries
stories.why: More than 230 real emergencies handled since March 2023, free of charge to families.
texts:
“We built the rescue network to give others what we didn’t have at the time,” says Nirit Rimon.

After her son Yanai drowned in a river in Mexico in 2021, she founded Haverim Mehalzim (Friends Rescuing Friends), a volunteer network that helps Israelis and Jews facing emergencies abroad. Since March 2023 it has handled more than 230 real emergencies in 49 countries, free of charge to families.

#Israel #Volunteers #Rescue #SocialImpact

More than 1,000 requests. Over 230 real emergencies. 49 countries.

That’s the record so far of Friends Rescuing Friends, an Israeli volunteer network run under the nonprofit Gvanim. Its co-CEO Ron Lavi estimates that about 35 of those cases would likely have ended in death without the network’s help. Families pay nothing.

#Israel #Volunteers #Rescue #SocialImpact

What if help were already nearby wherever you traveled?

Friends Rescuing Friends started as a WhatsApp group. Now volunteers around the world are alerted by country, a coordination center manages information, a forward team works on the ground with local rescue services, and lawyers and psychologists support families.

An idea any community could borrow.

#Israel #Volunteers #Rescue #SocialImpact
stories.og_title: 'Is he a Mossad agent?': Inside Israel's global volunteer rescue network

stories.teaser: Technion physicists steer electrons with light in 860 attoseconds
stories.headline: Technion physicists use shaped laser light to steer electron currents in bursts of 860 attoseconds
stories.why: Published in Nature Photonics; works at room temperature and in air.
texts:
Steering electrons with light.

Technion physicists led by Prof. Michael Kruger shaped two-color infrared laser pulses to control which way electrons flow between a microscope’s nanometric tip and a sample. The current bursts lasted just 860 attoseconds. Published in Nature Photonics.

“Finally we managed to prove beyond any doubt that we are able to control the direction of the current.”

#Israel #Technion #Physics #Science

860 attoseconds.

That’s how long the electron current bursts lasted in a new Technion experiment, published in Nature Photonics. Using a scanning tunneling microscope and shaped laser pulses, the team controlled the direction of electron flow with a resolution of about 2 nanometers, at room temperature and in air, without a vacuum.

#Israel #Technion #Physics #Science

Can light act as a switch for electricity?

At the Technion, Prof. Michael Kruger’s team showed it can steer electron currents in either direction, in bursts lasting 860 attoseconds. It took several years and three different laser systems.

“We tested three different laser systems, and rebuilt the optical setup many times,” says Dr. Adi Goldner.

#Israel #Technion #Physics #Science

stories.teaser: Did early humans collect souvenirs half a million years ago?
stories.headline: Tel Aviv University researchers suggest early humans in Israel kept souvenirs half a million years ago
stories.why: Published in Evolutionary Anthropology, based on finds from Qesem Cave, Revadim, Jaljulia and Sechin Valley.
texts:
The first keepsakes?

Tel Aviv University researchers suggest that early humans in what is now Israel may have collected personal souvenirs as far back as half a million years ago: small colorful pebbles at Qesem Cave, hand axes shaped around fossils, and old weathered flint tools kept rather than discarded. Published in Evolutionary Anthropology.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Archaeology #Prehistory

Half a million years ago, people may already have been holding on to memories.

A Tel Aviv University team spanning zoology, archaeology and psychology, including Dr. Yoav Ram and Prof. Ran Barkai, proposes that special objects found at Israeli prehistoric sites served as souvenirs, and may have shaped the evolution of autobiographical memory. The authors stress it is a hypothesis.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Archaeology #Prehistory

“An object like this may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives,” says Dr. Yoav Ram of Tel Aviv University.

The team looked at colorful pebbles, fossil-decorated hand axes and reused old flint tools from Qesem Cave and other Israeli sites, and suggests early humans kept them as keepsakes.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Archaeology #Prehistory

stories.teaser: Israeli-American AI that helps prevent blindness wins the Prix Galien
stories.headline: Israeli-American AEYE Health wins the Prix Galien USA award for AI that screens for diabetic eye disease
stories.why: Its FDA-cleared AEYE-DS gives near-immediate eye exam results without a physician reading the images.
texts:
AI that helps prevent blindness, now award-winning.

Israeli-American company AEYE Health won the 2026 Prix Galien USA Award for Best Digital Health Solution. Its FDA-cleared AEYE-DS performs diabetic eye exams autonomously, with portable or tabletop retinal cameras, giving near-immediate results without a physician interpreting the images. It was validated in three phase-III clinical trials.

#Israel #AI #HealthTech #Diabetes

Three phase-III clinical trials. FDA clearance. And now the Prix Galien.

AEYE Health’s AEYE-DS, invented by co-founder and CEO Dr. Zack Dvey-Aharon, was named Best Digital Health Solution at the 2026 Prix Galien USA Awards in New York. The fully autonomous AI screens for diabetic eye disease at virtually any point of care.

#Israel #AI #HealthTech #Diabetes

What if a diabetic eye exam didn’t need a specialist on hand?

That’s what AEYE-DS does, delivering results in moments from a retinal photo. The Israeli-American innovation just won the Prix Galien USA Award for Best Digital Health Solution.

“We are only at the beginning of what autonomous AI can accomplish for global healthcare,” says Dr. Zack Dvey-Aharon.

#Israel #AI #HealthTech #Diabetes
stories.og_title: Israeli-American AEYE Health wins Prix Galien Award for new AI technology helping prevent blindness

stories.teaser: An Israeli wearable incubator lets parents hold premature babies skin to skin
stories.headline: A wearable incubator from Israel’s Skincubator Neocare begins its first US trial, letting parents hold premature babies skin to skin
stories.why: FDA Breakthrough Device designation; the first US trial participant is at Children’s Memorial Hermann in Houston.
texts:
Holding your premature baby, safely.

The Skincubator, developed by Israeli company Skincubator Neocare, is a wearable incubator that lets parents keep premature babies skin to skin while they stay warm and connected to medical lines. A mother of twins at Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston is the first US trial participant.

“This is a great invention,” she says.

#Israel #MedTech #Preemies #Parenting

70–90% humidity, 84.2–87.8°F, and a parent’s heartbeat.

The Israeli-developed Skincubator keeps a premature baby in a warm, humid, enclosed space worn by a parent, with room for ventilator tubes and lines. In December 2025 it received FDA Breakthrough Device designation, and its first US trial is now underway in Houston.

#Israel #MedTech #Preemies #Parenting

What if an incubator didn’t have to keep parents and babies apart?

That was the idea behind the Skincubator, a wearable incubator from Israeli company Skincubator Neocare. Its creators spent four years designing it. Now families at Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston are the first in the US to try it in a trial.

#Israel #MedTech #Preemies #Parenting
stories.og_title: Parents of premature newborns can have more skin-to-skin contact with new device

stories.teaser: Israeli wildlife photographer Amit Eshel named best of 20 years
stories.headline: Israeli wildlife photographer Amit Eshel wins Photographer of the Year and the “Photographer of the 20 Years” title
stories.why: Two first-place category wins at the Golden Turtle competition, plus its top award and a historic title.
texts:
Arctic wolves, gelada monkeys, and a historic title.

Israeli wildlife photographer Amit Eshel won first place in two categories at the Golden Turtle international photography competition, was named Photographer of the Year, and received the title “Photographer of the 20 Years,” chosen by a near-unanimous jury vote.

“It is a tremendous privilege, and an excitement that is hard to describe in words.”

#Israel #Photography #Wildlife #Nature

Best photographer in 20 years of competition.

That’s the title Amit Eshel received at the Golden Turtle competition’s 20th anniversary, selected from all past Photographers of the Year and prize-winning finalists. He also won first place for a photo of gelada monkeys in Ethiopia and for a portrait of two Arctic wolves in Canada.

#Israel #Photography #Wildlife #Nature

What does it take to be the best in 20 years?

For Israeli photographer Amit Eshel: patient work from the Negev Desert to the Mongolian steppe and the Arctic. He was named Photographer of the Year and “Photographer of the 20 Years” at the Golden Turtle competition.

“It is without doubt one of the most exciting and meaningful moments in my career.”

#Israel #Photography #Wildlife #Nature

stories.teaser: An Israeli blood test spots early breast cancer with 95% accuracy
stories.headline: Weizmann and Hebrew University scientists develop a blood test that detects early breast cancer with 95% accuracy
stories.why: Published in Nature; it also predicted recurrence with 81% accuracy. Still experimental.
texts:
A blood test for early breast cancer.

Scientists led by Dr. Efrat Shema of the Weizmann Institute and Prof. Guy Ron of the Hebrew University developed an experimental blood test that detected early-stage breast cancer, in tumors under 2 cm, with 95% accuracy. Published in Nature.

“Breast cancer screening saves lives,” says Dr. Shema.

#Israel #Weizmann #BreastCancer #Health

95% accuracy for early tumors. 81% for predicting recurrence.

An Israeli blood test reads epigenetic marks on DNA-protein packages in the blood, using single-molecule microscopy and AI. Tested on 77 breast cancer patients and 30 healthy women, it caught early, localized tumors with 95% accuracy. The test is still experimental. Published in Nature.

#Israel #Weizmann #BreastCancer #Health

What if a blood draw could find breast cancer early?

Weizmann Institute and Hebrew University researchers, with Kaplan and Sheba medical centers, built an experimental test that does just that, with 95% accuracy for small, early tumors. It also predicted which patients’ cancer would return with 81% accuracy. The study was published in Nature.

#Israel #Weizmann #BreastCancer #Health
stories.og_title: Israeli blood test detects early breast cancer with 95% accuracy

stories.teaser: Weizmann scientists use DNA to make artificial materials move on their own
stories.headline: Weizmann Institute scientists use DNA to program artificial materials that move and pulse on their own
stories.why: Two studies, published in Nature Materials and Nature Physics.
texts:
Materials that move by themselves.

In Dr. Alexandra Tayar’s lab at the Weizmann Institute, researchers added DNA encoding a motor protein to a network of microtubules. The material made its own motors and began to move, forming growing bulges and then swirling for hours. The gene concentration controlled the timing and speed. Published in Nature Materials.

#Israel #Weizmann #Science #Materials

Two studies, two top journals.

Weizmann Institute researchers showed that DNA can program artificial “active” materials. In Nature Materials, a material produced its own motor proteins and moved on cue. In Nature Physics, long DNA strands formed a 3D network that made the material pulse in rhythmic oscillations, explained by a simple theoretical model.

#Israel #Weizmann #Science #Materials

Can you program a material the way you program a cell?

“We turned familiar biological variables, such as gene expression rate or a genetic feedback loop, into physical variables,” says Dr. Alexandra Tayar of the Weizmann Institute.

The team’s DNA-driven materials moved, braked on command and pulsed at regular intervals.

#Israel #Weizmann #Science #Materials
stories.og_title: לראשונה: DNA מעורר חומרים מלאכותיים לחיים ומסנכרן את תנועתם
